title: You forgot
hookLine: when troubled, you've forgotten that each person's mind shares in the divine (Meditations 12.26)

lines: WHY DID I COME IN HERE?
NOT NEW IDEAS. OLD ONES, DROPPED.
cards: You walk into the kitchen and stand there. Why did you come in? You knew a second ago.
Marcus thought being upset is a lot like that: not that you never knew the truth, but that it slipped out of your hand on the way in.
So in book twelve he writes himself a list, not of new ideas, but of things he already knew and kept forgetting the moment someone annoyed him.

teach.b: Meditations 12.26 opens, in plain words: when you're troubled by something, you've forgotten. Then he lists what. First, the list.
You've forgotten that all things happen by the nature of the whole. That another person's wrong is theirs, not yours. That what's happening now has happened before and will again.
That you're kin to every human being, not by blood or seed but by sharing in mind. Even yesterday's line is there: everything is opinion.

teach.h: EACH MIND SHARES IN THE DIVINE.
teach.b: Second, the line at the center: each person's mind, he says, is a god, and has flowed from there. The Greek word for mind is nous.

For the Stoics, a divine reason runs through the whole world, and every human mind is a piece of it, a spark from the same fire. Readers take this differently. Some hear something close to religious faith.

Some hear a poetic way of saying every person can reason, and so deserves respect. Marcus himself sometimes isn't sure what runs the world, as we saw a few days ago. Third, why it's in a list about being troubled.

teach.h: YOUR ANGER IS AIMED AT A RELATIVE.
teach.b: If the person who cut you off in traffic carries the same spark you do, your anger is aimed at a relative, a cousin in reason. That doesn't excuse what they did. It changes who you think you're dealing with.
Fourth, the comfort in the word forgot.
You don't need to become someone new.
You need to remember what you already knew, which is why Marcus kept writing it down.

how: Readers of the Meditations often use 12.26 as a checklist when upset, running through Marcus's reminders, among them that every person's mind shares in the same reason.

o: Marcus's scolding for anyone who neglects their duties
Marcus's diagnosis: when troubled, you've dropped what you knew
a reminder that memory fades with age, even for emperors

p: shared mind, not blood or seed

s: in 12.26 Marcus lists brand-new ideas he's never written before
the list gathers reminders from earlier pages, even all is opinion.
Marcus says each person's mind is a god and has flowed from there
for the Stoics, every human mind is a piece of the reason running through the world.
all readers agree on what Marcus means by the divine
some hear religious faith, some hear a way of saying every person can reason.

games.q: someone cuts you off in traffic and you're furious. what does 12.26 say you've forgotten?
o: that this person shares in the same reason you do.
games.why: Marcus says when we're troubled we've forgotten our kinship: a community of mind, not of blood.

practice: Bring to mind one person who's been hard to deal with lately, and try Marcus's reminder on them: this person has a mind, a spark of the same reason that's in you; they worry, they plan, they get things wrong.
If you hold something sacred, let that word sit beside them for a moment; if you don't, let the word kin sit there, and notice whether anything shifts.

wordCard.voice: You forgot. Marcus's line for every troubled moment: you didn't lack the truth, you dropped it, including that each person's mind shares in the divine. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: mind, intelligence. Marcus says each person's nous is a god, flowed from the whole.

carryVoice: Your line: I forgot. Remembering again is enough; you don't need anything new. Until tomorrow.
